tooley.explain: Tooley 14.4.2: periodic is continuously repetitive; aperiodic is predictable but not continuous; random is totally unpredictable.
tooley.detail:
Tooley 14.4.2: periodic noise repeats continuously, aperiodic noise is predictable but not continuous (for example switching pulses), random noise is totally unpredictable. A-periodic means no regular period.

Scale of predictability: periodic > aperiodic > random.

tooley.q: EMI can be conveyed from a source to a receiver by:
tooley.explain: The energy can be conducted through wiring and metallic structure, or radiated through air, plastic and fibreglass (Tooley 14.4.1).
tooley.detail:
EMI travels by two routes: conduction through wiring and metallic structure, or radiation through air, plastic and fibreglass. The one-route options miss the other, so both countermeasures (screening and filtering) are needed.

Conducted: filter; radiated: screen.

tooley.q: The display produced by a spectrum analyser shows:
tooley.explain: A spectrum analyser plots signal level (amplitude) against frequency; amplitude against time is an oscilloscope.
tooley.detail:
A spectrum analyser plots amplitude (signal level) against frequency, so each noise component can be seen. An oscilloscope plots amplitude against time. No simple instrument plots frequency against time (that is a spectrogram).

Horizontal axis: frequency.

tooley.q: EMI can be reduced by means of:
tooley.explain: All of screening, bonding/grounding and filtering reduce EMI (Tooley 14.4.3, 14.6).
tooley.detail:
The three EMI countermeasure groups are screening, bonding/grounding and filtering. Using only one or two is incomplete because each handles a different path.

The lecture slides also add cable separation and ferrite cores.

tooley.q: The effects of HIRF can be reduced by:
tooley.explain: Tooley 14.6: grounding and bonding help minimise the effects of high-intensity radio-frequency fields (HIRF), together with screening and filtering.
tooley.detail:
HIRF is reduced by the same trio: screening, bonding and filtering. Bonding provides a low-impedance current path, screening keeps the external field off the wiring, filtering removes what gets in.

HIRF = high-intensity radiated fields from outside.

tooley.q: The typical maximum value of bonding resistance is:
tooley.explain: Bonding resistance must be very low (Tooley 14.6 says below 0.001 to 0.003 Ω; the lecture slide says 0.001 to 0.003 Ω); option (a) is the one that fits.
tooley.detail:
Bonding resistance must be tiny (milliohm order) so lightning and static current flows without creating a potential difference. Only "below 0.005 Ω" is in a reasonable range; the other two give far larger resistances.

Warning: Tooley and the lecture quote different thresholds (0.001 to 0.003 Ω), so use only the order of magnitude.

tooley.q: Effective protection against lightning and static discharge damage to an aircraft requires that:
opts: all power and bus cables must be well insulated
all isolated conducting parts must have high resistance to ground
all parts of the metal structure of the aircraft must be bonded to ground
tooley.explain: A low-impedance path is needed for lightning and static current: bond the whole metal structure, leave no isolated conductors.
tooley.detail:
All parts of the metal structure must be bonded to ground so there is a low-impedance path for lightning and static discharge current; an isolated conductor can charge up and spark. Cable insulation does not provide a current path.

Rule: no "floating" conductors.

tooley.q: Supply-borne noise can be eliminated by means of:
tooley.explain: The supply is DC or 400 Hz, so a low-pass filter keeps the supply and blocks high-frequency noise.
tooley.detail:
The supply is DC or 400 Hz (low frequency) while supply-borne noise is high frequency, so a low-pass filter keeps the supply and blocks the noise. High-pass and band-pass filters would block the supply.

RC cutoff: f = 1/(2πRC), for example 1 kΩ and 100 nF gives 1.59 kHz.

tooley.q: Noise generated by a switching circuit is worse when:
opts: switching is slow and current is high
switching is fast and current is high
switching is fast and current is low
tooley.explain: More electromagnetic energy is released when the change in signal level and its rate increase (Tooley 14.4.2).
tooley.detail:
Emission is strongest when the signal level changes a lot and fast: fast switching with a large current gives a high di/dt. Slow switching or small current both reduce emission.

Countermeasures: slow the edges, use capacitors or a snubber.

floyd.q: According to Floyd, how is crosstalk minimised?
opts: Using twisted-pair cables so the fields cancel
Using bare wire only to cut capacitance
Using only cable with a very thick insulating jacket
floyd.explain: The two wires in each pair are twisted so that they cross at nearly 90° and cancel the electromagnetic fields generated by the signals.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.13 · section 13-1, Figure 13-4 (p.741; Section Checkup)
floyd.detail:
The two wires of a twisted pair cross at nearly 90° so the fields from each wire's signal cancel, reducing crosstalk. Bare wire or thick insulation alone does not cancel fields.

Self-Test 1 in Module 08 asks the same thing.

floyd.q: Which Floyd cable type gives more EMI protection with a metal sleeve?
floyd.explain: Floyd: STP is encased in a metal sleeve and gives more protection from EMI; UTP is limited to low-noise environments and lower frequencies.
floyd.detail:
STP has a surrounding metal sleeve so it protects better against EMI but is costlier and heavier than UTP. UTP suits low-noise environments and lower frequencies (up to about 1 MHz).

Choose: high noise STP, low noise UTP.

floyd.q: How are current and voltage spikes on the VCC and ground lines of digital circuits absorbed?
opts: Decoupling capacitors from VCC to ground
floyd.explain: Floyd: use about a 1 µF capacitor for the whole board and small 0.022 to 0.1 µF capacitors distributed near fast-switching devices.
floyd.detail:
Fast-switching digital circuits draw pulses of current from the supply so VCC spikes. A decoupling capacitor from VCC to ground supplies local current and absorbs the spikes; place it close to the IC power pin. Raising the supply resistance makes spikes worse.

Combine: a 1 µF bulk capacitor with 0.022 to 0.1 µF small ones.

floyd.q: The HIGH-level noise margin V_NH of a logic gate is defined as:
floyd.explain: Equation 15-1; V_NL = V_IL(max) − V_OL(max) is Equation 15-2.
floyd.detail:
The high-level noise margin V_NH = V_OH(min) − V_IH(min): the margin between the minimum high that the driving gate delivers and the minimum high the receiving gate accepts. The low level is V_NL = V_IL(max) − V_OL(max). The other options mix the wrong quantities.

Remember: output minus input at the same level.

floyd.q: A TTL gate has VIH(min) = 2.25 V and VIL(max) = 0.65 V and is driven by a gate with VOH(min) = 2.4 V and VOL(max) = 0.4 V. The HIGH- and LOW-level noise margins are:
floyd.explain: V_NH = 2.4 − 2.25 = 0.15 V; V_NL = 0.65 − 0.4 = 0.25 V (matches the printed answer).
floyd.detail:
V_NH = V_OH(min) − V_IH(min) = 2.4 − 2.25 = 0.15 V; V_NL = V_IL(max) − V_OL(max) = 0.65 − 0.4 = 0.25 V. 2.4 V and 0.4 V are just output levels, not noise margins.

A small noise margin means noise can flip the level easily.

floyd.q: A gate with V_IL(max) = 0.8 V is driven by a gate with V_OL(max) = 0.4 V. The LOW-level noise margin is:
floyd.detail:
This is Floyd Equation 15-2. Adding instead of subtracting gives 1.2 V, which is wrong; 0.8 V is just V_IL(max).

The noise margin is the largest noise that can be added while the gate still reads a LOW correctly.

floyd.q: A driving gate has V_OH(min) = 2.4 V and the receiving gate has V_IH(min) = 2.0 V. The HIGH-level noise margin is:
floyd.detail: Equation 15-1: minimum output minus minimum input at the same HIGH level. 4.4 V is a meaningless sum; 2.0 V is just the input threshold.

floyd.q: Twisted-pair cable reduces crosstalk because the fields from the two wires cancel.
floyd.detail: The wires cross at nearly 90° so the flux from opposite currents cancels. Slide 29 also lists twisted or screened wires first among the EMC improvements.

floyd.q: A decoupling capacitor placed far from the IC's supply pin is just as effective as one placed close.
floyd.explain: False: it must be placed close to the supply pin.
floyd.detail: A long lead adds parasitic inductance so the capacitor cannot supply fast current pulses. Floyd 6-11 recommends small capacitors distributed near the fast-switching devices.

generated.q: What is 0.5 W in dBm?
opts: 30 dBm because 0.5 W is close to 1 W
generated.detail:
10 log(0.5 W/1 mW) = 10 log 500 = 26.99, about 27 dBm. 30 dBm is 1 W and −3 dBm is half a mW. Anchors: 0 dBm = 1 mW, 30 dBm = 1 W.

Quick rule: each ×10 of power is +10 dB.

generated.q: A cable has −2 dB loss and 1 V input. The output voltage is about:
generated.explain: V_out = 10^(−2/20) × 1 V = 0.794 V (0.631 is the wrong result from using the factor 10).
generated.detail:
For voltage: V_out = V_in × 10^(dB/20) = 10^(−0.1) = 0.794 V. 0.631 results from using 10 instead of 20 (the power formula).

Voltage uses 20 log, power uses 10 log.

generated.q: An amplifier of +40 dB has 10 W input. The output power is:
opts: 10 kW as printed on the slide
generated.explain: 10 W × 10^(40/10) = 10 × 10⁴ = 100,000 W. Slide 21 mistakenly prints 10 kW.
generated.detail:
+40 dB in power is ×10⁴, 10 W × 10,000 = 100 kW. Slide 21's 10 kW is wrong (off by a factor of 10). 400 W confuses adding with multiplying.

Check: +10 dB ×10, +20 dB ×100, +30 dB ×1000, +40 dB ×10⁴.

generated.q: An input level of −20 dBm goes through a +30 dB amplifier. The output level is:
generated.detail:
A dBm level adds directly to a dB gain: −20 + 30 = +10 dBm = 10 mW. −50 dBm subtracts by mistake and 30 dBm ignores the input level.

Do not add dBm to dBm; only dBm plus dB.

generated.q: A tenfold increase in voltage is how many dB?
generated.explain: 20 log 10 = 20 dB (a tenfold power increase would be 10 dB).
generated.detail:
A tenfold voltage increase gives 20 log 10 = +20 dB. A tenfold power increase is +10 dB. +100 dB is ×10⁵ in voltage.

Squaring: power ∝ V², so the factor 20 is double the factor 10.

generated.q: A 50 V, 2 kHz square wave (V/n form). The fifth harmonic has amplitude and frequency:
generated.explain: 50/5 = 10 V; 5 × 2 kHz = 10 kHz (Tooley TYU 14.1).
generated.detail:
A square wave has only odd harmonics with amplitude V/n (in Tooley's form, V is the fundamental amplitude). Fifth harmonic: 50/5 = 10 V at 5 × 2 kHz = 10 kHz. 5 kHz divides the frequency by mistake.

Even harmonics of a symmetric square wave are zero.

generated.q: A 100 nF capacitor with 10 nH ESL has a resonant frequency of about:
generated.detail:
f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π√(10 nH × 100 nF)) = 1/(2π × 3.16×10⁻⁸) = 5.03 MHz. 50 kHz and 500 MHz are off by a factor of 100.

The smaller the ESL, the higher the resonance, so small capacitors serve high frequencies.

generated.q: Above its resonant frequency a real capacitor behaves as:
opts: A quality standard for flight control software
A mandatory government EMC regulation for aircraft
A test procedure published by the RTCA, not a requirement
generated.explain: Above f_r the ESL dominates and Z rises with frequency (slide 36).
generated.detail:
Below f_r a real capacitor is a capacitor; above f_r the parasitic inductance ESL dominates so Z = ωL rises with frequency and the capacitor acts as an inductor, a poor filter. It never becomes a pure resistor over a wide band.

That is why a large and a small capacitor are used in parallel.

generated.q: What is DO-160?
opts: A test procedure published by the RTCA, not a requirement
generated.explain: Slide 27: DO-160 is a test procedure; DO-178 is the software one.
generated.detail:
DO-160 is an environmental (including EMC) test procedure published by the RTCA; it does not set requirements itself, those come from certification rules. The software standard is DO-178.

Three standards: DO-160 (test), DO-178 (software), DO-254 (hardware).

generated.q: The CISPR 11 Group 1 Class A radiated emission limit above 230 MHz (at 30 m) is:
opts: Banning Wi-Fi devices while the engines run for the purpose of flight
Switching off all displays whenever the Wi-Fi system is on
Adding ferrite cores to every cockpit display
generated.explain: Slide 26: 30 dBµV/m from 30 to 230 MHz, 37 dBµV/m above 230 MHz.
generated.detail:
CISPR 11 Group 1 Class A, measured at 30 m: 30 dBµV/m for 30 to 230 MHz and 37 dBµV/m above 230 MHz. 47 dBµV/m is a different limit (another measuring distance).

Check the measuring distance when comparing limits.

generated.q: Wi-Fi interfered with displays on the Boeing 757. The measure stated on the cockpit placard is:
opts: Ferrite only blocks very low frequencies so it ignores the signal
The currents in the two wires are opposite, so the flux in the core cancels
Ferrite has no magnetic property so it acts on nothing
generated.explain: Slide 3: the placard bans Wi-Fi devices on the flight deck while the engines run.
generated.detail:
On the Boeing 757, Wi-Fi devices interfered with the displays, so the cockpit placard bans Wi-Fi while the engines run for flight purposes. Ferrite is a different technical fix, not the placard's content.

A typical example of EMI from personal devices.

generated.q: Why does a ferrite core not affect the wanted differential signal?
opts: The currents in the two wires are opposite so the flux in the core cancels
generated.explain: Slide 32: in differential mode the flux cancels and impedance is low; in common mode the flux adds and impedance is high.
generated.detail:
The two signal wires carry opposite currents so the flux in the ferrite cancels: low impedance, the signal is unimpeded. Common-mode noise has same-direction currents so the flux adds, high impedance, it is blocked.

Ferrite filters common-mode noise without affecting the signal.

generated.q: What is 1 W in dBm?
generated.explain: 10 log(1 W/1 mW) = 10 log 1000 = 30 dBm.
generated.detail:
dBm is referenced to 1 mW: 0 dBm = 1 mW. 1 W is 1000 times 1 mW, so 10 × 3 = 30 dBm. 0 dBm is 1 mW, not 1 W.

Anchors: 0 dBm = 1 mW, 30 dBm = 1 W, 60 dBm = 1 kW.

generated.q: Adding 3 dB of gain changes the power by about:
generated.detail:
G = 10^(dB/10) gives 1.995 for 3 dB. A factor of three would be 4.77 dB. dB is a ratio so it never adds a fixed number of watts.

Conversely −3 dB leaves half.

generated.q: A level of −90 dBm is a power of:
generated.detail:
−90 dBm = 10⁻⁹ mW, and 1 mW = 10⁻³ W so it equals 10⁻¹² W = 1 pW. The third option contradicts itself: 10⁻⁹ mW is not 1 µW. This is the power scale of a weak-signal receiver (Tooley Figure 14.9).

Do not forget to convert mW to W.

generated.q: A voltage ratio of 0.5 (halved) is:
generated.detail: Voltage uses 20 log: 20 × (−0.301) = −6.02 dB. −3 dB is power halved. Since power ∝ V², half the voltage gives a quarter of the power (−6 dB).

generated.q: A 1 kHz square wave contains harmonics at:
generated.explain: A symmetric square wave has only odd harmonics, with amplitude V/n.
generated.detail:
The Fourier series of a square wave: (4V/π)(sin ωt + sin 3ωt/3 + sin 5ωt/5 + ...). The steeper the edge, the stronger the high harmonics, so fast pulses emit broadband noise. A single frequency belongs only to a sine wave.

This is why slowing the edges reduces EMI.

generated.q: A 1 µF capacitor with 10 nH ESL has a resonant frequency of about:
generated.detail: √(10⁻¹⁴) = 10⁻⁷ so f_r = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁷) = 1.59 MHz. 5.03 MHz is the result for 100 nF. A larger capacitor resonates lower: it filters well at low frequency but turns inductive sooner.

generated.q: What best protects a sensitive signal wire from an external electric-field disturbance?
opts: Running it parallel to a power cable
A screen grounded at least at one end
Coiling the wire into a large loop
generated.explain: A grounded screen diverts the interference to ground.
generated.detail:
A screen acts as a Faraday cage for electric fields. A large loop increases the pickup area for magnetic fields, and running parallel to a power cable increases coupling. Grounding both ends protects better at high frequency but can create a ground loop at low frequency.

Rule: separate cables, twist the pair and screen.

generated.q: A ground loop occurs when:
opts: all equipment shares a single ground point
a screen is grounded at two points at different potentials, creating a path for interference current
generated.explain: The ground potential difference drives current through the screen.
generated.detail: Two ground points on an aircraft can differ in potential due to return currents, so current flows in the screen and couples into the signal. Single-point grounding avoids the loop. Twisting is a magnetic-noise reduction measure, not a cause.

generated.q: In lightning protection, which provision keeps the fuel system safe from a strike?
opts: Electrical bonding of the whole structure and avoiding gaps that could spark
generated.explain: Bonding the whole structure gives the lightning current a continuous path.
generated.detail:
Lightning peak current is 10 to 200 kA (slide 11); gaps in the path produce sparks next to the fuel. Insulating shells provide no current path and removing grounding straps does the opposite.

Same principle as Tooley chapter 14 question 7; slide 44 adds preventing static build-up in fuel.

generated.q: An RC low-pass filter with R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF has a cutoff of:
generated.detail:
RC = 1000 × 100×10⁻⁹ = 10⁻⁴ s. f_c = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴) = 1591 Hz. 159 Hz corresponds to C = 1 µF and 15.9 kHz to C = 10 nF.

At f_c the amplitude is down 3 dB.

generated.q: In conducted noise, common-mode noise differs from differential-mode in that:
opts: the interference current flows in opposite directions on the two wires
the interference current flows in the same direction on both wires relative to ground
generated.explain: Common mode: in phase on both wires; differential: opposite phase.
generated.detail: A ferrite core around both wires blocks common mode (flux adds) without impeding the differential signal (flux cancels). Differential mode is the mode of the wanted signal so ferrite cannot filter it out.

generated.q: What reduces interference radiated from a power cable into a signal cable?
opts: Separate them and cross at right angles
generated.explain: Coupling falls with distance and depends on direction.
generated.detail: Crossing at right angles means the flux of one cable does not pass through the loop of the other so coupling is almost zero. Bundling and running parallel give maximum coupling; slide 39 lists separating power and signal cables.
